shots.title: Typical 401(k) & IRA balance, by age
shots.src: Nest Egg Atlas calculation from the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances public data (survey weights) · retirement accounts = 401(k), IRA and similar · 2025 dollars
shots.narration: Here's what the typical American household actually has in its 401(k)s and IRAs, by age, from the Federal Reserve's newest survey. {p} Under thirty-five: about twenty-one thousand dollars. Thirty-five to forty-four: about sixty-one thousand. Forty-five to fifty-four: about a hundred and thirty-two thousand. {p} Fifty-five to sixty-four: about two hundred and thirty-nine thousand. {p} Sixty-five to seventy-four, and seventy-five and older: about two hundred and fifty-seven thousand. {pp} Those are medians, for households that have an account, in 2025 dollars, with every retirement account in the household added together. And that last part, having an account, matters more than you might think.

Because about half of households in their late sixties and early seventies don't have one at all. {p} In this video, we'll go through who has a retirement account, what the typical balance really is, why the average you see in headlines is so misleading, and what these balances actually pay in retirement, and how your own number compares. {pp} <soft>As always, this is education, not financial advice.</soft>

shots.title: Households with any retirement account
shots.src: Nest Egg Atlas calculation from the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances public data (survey weights) · retirement accounts = 401(k), IRA and similar · 2025 dollars
shots.narration: First: who has one at all. {p} Across all American households, about fifty-five percent have money in a retirement account like a 401(k) or an IRA. {p} The share peaks in the working years: about sixty-three percent of households between forty-five and sixty-four. {p} Then it drops. About forty-nine percent at sixty-five to seventy-four. About forty-five percent at seventy-five and older. {pp} So in the sixty-five to seventy-four group, slightly more than half of households have no retirement account at all. That means the household right in the middle of that age group has zero in a 401(k) or IRA.

Why does the share fall after sixty-five? {p} Some households spend their accounts down, or move the money elsewhere. {p} Required minimum distributions now start at seventy-three, so money has to come out of most of these accounts every year after that. {p} And many of today's oldest retirees spent their careers with traditional pensions, before 401(k)s became common in the 1980s and 90s. For them, the pension check is the retirement plan. {pp} None of those pensions show up in these numbers. Neither does Social Security.

shots.title: Age 65–74, households with an account
shots.sub: Balance at each point of the ladder · 2025
shots.src: Nest Egg Atlas calculation from the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances public data (survey weights) · retirement accounts = 401(k), IRA and similar · 2025 dollars
shots.narration: Now the balances. Let's focus on households aged sixty-five to seventy-four that do have an account. {p} A quarter of them have less than about ninety-four thousand dollars. {p} Half have less than about two hundred and fifty-seven thousand. That's the median. {p} A quarter have more than about eight hundred and thirty-seven thousand. {p} And the top ten percent have more than about one point nine five million. {pp} For fifty-five to sixty-four, just before retirement, the median is about two hundred and thirty-nine thousand, and the top ten percent start at about one point eight five million. {p} At seventy-five and older, the median is also about two hundred and fifty-seven thousand, and the top quarter starts at about nine hundred and seventy-eight thousand.

So if you're in your late sixties, have a 401(k) or IRA, and it holds a quarter of a million dollars, you're right in the middle of your peers. {p} If it holds a hundred thousand, you're near the bottom quarter of account holders, but still ahead of the roughly half of households your age who have nothing in these accounts at all. {p} That's a far more useful benchmark than the averages in most headlines.

shots.title: Age 65–74, households with an account
shots.src: Nest Egg Atlas calculation from the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances public data (survey weights) · retirement accounts = 401(k), IRA and similar · 2025 dollars
shots.narration: Now, the number you usually see in headlines: the average. {p} That's the median, from before: about two hundred and fifty-seven thousand. {p} The average balance for the same households is about seven hundred and sixty-eight thousand dollars. Three times the median. {pp} Why so different? Because a small group of very large accounts pulls the average up. A few households with several million dollars move the average a lot, but they don't move the median at all. {p} So when you read that the average retiree has three quarters of a million dollars in a 401(k), remember: well over half of retirees with an account have far less than that. Most likely around seven in ten. {p} For fifty-five to sixty-four, it's the same story: an average of about six hundred and seventy thousand, against a median of about two hundred and thirty-nine thousand.

That's not just a quirk of statistics. It changes how you should read your own number. {p} Comparing yourself to the average will almost always make you feel behind. Comparing yourself to the median tells you where you really stand. {p} And comparing yourself to people your own age matters too: a sixty-eight-year-old and a forty-five-year-old are in completely different places.

shots.title: Households 65–74 with at least…
shots.sub: In retirement accounts · share of ALL households, 2025
shots.src: Nest Egg Atlas calculation from the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances public data (survey weights) · retirement accounts = 401(k), IRA and similar · 2025 dollars
shots.narration: Here's another way to see it, counting every household, with or without an account. {p} Among households aged sixty-five to seventy-four, about thirty-six percent have at least a hundred thousand dollars in retirement accounts. {p} About one in four has at least two hundred and fifty thousand. {p} About eighteen percent, half a million. {p} And about eleven and a half percent, a million or more. Roughly one in nine. {pp} For fifty-five to sixty-four, the shares are a little higher: about forty percent have a hundred thousand or more, and about twelve percent a million. {p} Seventy-five and older: about thirty-one percent have a hundred thousand or more, and about eleven percent a million.

And at the bottom: about half of all households aged sixty-five to seventy-four have nothing in these accounts. For most of them, retirement income comes from Social Security, sometimes a pension, home equity, and work. {p} That's why Social Security matters so much. For many retirees, the lifetime value of their checks is worth more than everything in their accounts, even though it never shows up on a balance sheet. And Social Security checks rise with inflation every year, which no savings account can promise.

shots.title: What the median balance pays
shots.sub: Age 65–74 · 4% rule of thumb · before taxes
shots.src: 4% rule of thumb (Bengen, 1994): first-year withdrawal of 4% of savings · Social Security Administration, 2027 COLA Fact Sheet · illustration, not advice

stats.at: eight hundred and fifty-seven dollars a month
stats.label: per month from $257k (4%)

stats.at: two thousand one hundred and seventy dollars a month
stats.label: average Social Security check, 2027

shots.narration: So what does the median balance actually pay? {p} Using the common four percent rule of thumb, a balance of two hundred and fifty-seven thousand dollars supports a first-year withdrawal of about ten thousand two hundred and eighty dollars. That's about eight hundred and fifty-seven dollars a month, before taxes. {p} Compare that with Social Security. In 2027, the average retired worker's check is about two thousand one hundred and seventy dollars a month. {pp} So for the typical household with an account, Social Security pays about two and a half times more than the 401(k) does.

Two more things to keep in mind. {p} First, money in traditional, pre-tax accounts is taxed as income when you take it out. Two hundred and fifty-seven thousand dollars in a traditional IRA is not two hundred and fifty-seven thousand dollars to spend. {p} Second, these are household numbers. A married couple counts once, with both spouses' accounts added together. So for a couple, the typical balance per person is even smaller. {p} And if your money is in a Roth IRA or a Roth 401(k), qualified withdrawals are tax-free, so the same balance goes further.

items.text: Pre-tax = taxed on the way out

shots.title: The ladder, age 65–74
shots.src: Nest Egg Atlas calculation from the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances public data (survey weights) · retirement accounts = 401(k), IRA and similar · 2025 dollars
shots.narration: So here's the quick ladder for sixty-five to seventy-four. {p} Zero: about half of all households. {p} About ninety-four thousand: the bottom quarter of those with an account. {p} About two hundred and fifty-seven thousand: the middle. {p} About eight hundred and thirty-seven thousand: the top quarter. {p} About one point nine five million: the top ten percent. {pp} If you're somewhere between two rungs, you're in very normal company. Most people are. {p} Wherever you are on this ladder, remember that it leaves out Social Security, pensions and your home.

items.at: About one point nine five million

items.text: NOT COUNTED: SOCIAL SECURITY, PENSIONS, HOME

shots.narration: Tell me in the comments: does your balance surprise you, compared with these numbers? {p} And if you're already retired, I'd like to know: was it a 401(k), an IRA, or a pension that did most of the work? {p} And if you know someone your age who's worried they're behind, send them this. The median might be a relief.
For most retirees, the biggest piece is still Social Security. To see when it pays to claim, watch this next. {p} This is Nest Egg Atlas. See you next time.

voice.style: You are the narrator of a calm, trustworthy personal-finance documentary for Americans in their fifties, sixties and seventies. Read the script below in a warm, mature, unhurried voice, at about 138 words per minute, like a respected public-radio journalist explaining numbers to a friend. Let each dollar figure land with a short pause before it. Sound reassuring and clear, never salesy, never alarmed, never like an advertisement.

yt.title: 401(k) and IRA Balances at 55, 65 and 75: The Fed's New Numbers
yt.description:
What does the typical American household actually have in its 401(k)s and IRAs? Using the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, we calculate who has a retirement account by age, the median and the percentiles for households with one, why the average is three times the median, the share with $100k, $250k, $500k and $1 million, and what the median balance pays under the 4% rule compared with Social Security.

Educational content, not financial advice.

Sources: Federal Reserve Board, 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, summary extract public data (our calculation with survey weights; 2025 dollars); Social Security Administration, 2027 COLA Fact Sheet; Bengen (1994), 4% rule of thumb.
{music_credits}
Narration is AI-generated.
